subject: Cloud Computing
title: Linux: The Cloud's Operating System
description: A 60-second lesson on Linux: The Cloud's Operating System.

hook.text: A Finnish student posted his hobby project online in 1991. It now runs 96% of cloud servers.

buildup.text: Linus Torvalds created Linux as a free alternative to expensive Unix systems.

discovery.text: Linux is free, customizable, and endlessly adaptable — everything cloud providers need.

twist.text: Microsoft once called Linux a cancer. Now Azure runs more Linux than Windows.

climax.text: Without Linux, cloud computing as we know it wouldn't exist. It's the invisible backbone.

punchline.text: A student's side project powers the modern internet.

quiz.question: What percentage of cloud servers run Linux?

details.summary: Linux runs the vast majority of cloud workloads because it is free, open-source, highly customizable, and extremely reliable. Cloud providers modify Linux kernels for optimal performance, and most cloud-native tools and technologies assume a Linux environment.
details.whyItMatters: Linux's dominance in the cloud means understanding Linux is essential for cloud computing. Its open-source nature allowed cloud providers to customize it freely without licensing costs.
takeaways: Linux runs over 90 percent of cloud workloads
Its open-source license eliminated per-instance OS costs
Cloud providers customize Linux kernels for their hardware

faq.question: Why did Linux win the cloud?
faq.answer: Linux is free to use and modify, eliminating per-instance licensing costs critical for cloud economics. Its stability, security, and flexibility made it ideal for server workloads. Cloud providers could customize the kernel for their specific hardware and workload patterns.

faq.question: What about Windows in the cloud?
faq.answer: Windows remains important for enterprise workloads, especially Microsoft-stack applications. Azure offers extensive Windows support, and AWS runs many Windows instances. However, Linux's cost advantage and container ecosystem make it the default choice for new cloud workloads.
